title: The lazy monk
hook: a legend: Shantideva, thought lazy, is asked to recite, and recites a masterpiece

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddhaghosa and his Path of Purification: virtue, concentration, wisdom. Your line was the path mapped. Where were you standing on the map? Day nine hundred sixty-six.

A busy house can have one person who never seems to do anything. At the great monastery of Nalanda, the legend says, that person was a young monk named Shantideva. The others saw him eat, sleep and wander, and never study. Tradition says they gave him a teasing nickname for it. So they hatched a plan to embarrass him into leaving. They would invite him to give a public recitation, in front of everyone, and let him fail. Today, the lazy monk.
screen: `A MONK WHO SEEMS TO DO NOTHING.` → `A PLAN TO EMBARRASS HIM.` → `A PUBLIC RECITATION.`

segments.voice: First, the trap. In the Tibetan telling, the monks set up a high teaching seat, some say on purpose without steps, and gathered a crowd to watch. Shantideva arrived, settled onto the seat without trouble, and asked a calm question. Shall I recite something old, or something new? Second, the surprise. They asked for something new, expecting nothing. And he began to recite the Bodhicharyavatara, the Way of the Bodhisattva: verses on the joy of the awakening mind, on patience, on effort, on meditation, on wisdom. The crowd went quiet. The lazy one spoke, and what came out was a masterpiece. Third, the vanishing. The legend says that when he reached the chapter on wisdom, at the verse where neither something nor nothing remains before the mind, he rose into the air and disappeared from sight, while his voice went on reciting. His work was gathered afterward from those who had heard it. Fourth, what the legend teaches. Nobody knew what was going on inside him. Quiet is not the same as empty. And that fits the week behind us. Aryadeva, the student who carried it. Asanga, whose eyes compassion opened. Vasubandhu, who changed his mind. Yogacara and the mind that colors everything. Logic asking how you know. Buddhaghosa's map. And now a monk everyone had judged, wrongly. Tomorrow we open one of his teachings.
screen: `A HIGH SEAT, A CROWD.` · `SOMETHING OLD, OR SOMETHING NEW?` · `HE RISES, AND HIS VOICE GOES ON.` · `QUIET IS NOT EMPTY.` · then, large: `THE LAZY ONE SPOKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: surprise someone kindly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you may have quietly written off. A coworker who seems checked out. A relative who never says much. Picture them for a moment with whole rooms inside them that you've never seen. Then think of one small, kind surprise you could give them today. A thank-you, a real question, a bit of help they didn't ask for. Choose it, and rest with it. The bell holds the time.
The lazy monk. The legend of Shantideva at Nalanda, judged idle, who was asked to recite and gave the Way of the Bodhisattva. Today's word.
Your line: the lazy one spoke. Today, when you're tempted to sum someone up, leave a little room for the masterpiece you haven't heard yet. That's the week. Day nine hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva is studied and recited in Tibetan Buddhism, and teachers tell the legend of his recitation at Nalanda when introducing the text.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a slacker.
what it means: a legend of a monk everyone judged idle, who, asked to recite, gave the Way of the Bodhisattva.
what a scholar hears: Tibetan tellings of Shantideva at Nalanda; at the verse where neither something nor nothing remains before the mind, he rises and vanishes.

sources.ref: Tibetan accounts of Shantideva's life (e.g., Buton's and Taranatha's histories)
Bodhicharyavatara 9.34 (neither something nor nothing remains before the mind)

notes: Told throughout as a legend. Details from Tibetan accounts (Buton, Taranatha): the nickname Bhusuku (traditionally explained as one who only eats, sleeps and strolls), the monks' plan, the high seat (in some versions without steps), the question 'old or new', rising into the sky at 9.34 with his voice continuing. The nickname itself is not spoken; confirm the paraphrase.
Chapter themes listed (awakening mind, patience, effort, meditation, wisdom) are a selection, not the full list of chapters; confirm.

'His work was gathered afterward from those who had heard it': some versions describe differing remembered versions and Shantideva later indicating where the text was kept; simplified. Confirm or cut.
Week end (days 960–966): the teach looks back over the week.
Audit: read in full; the 'old or new' question, the high seat and the vanishing at 9.34 match the Tibetan tellings; week recap matches days 960–965; no change.
